title: When Legal Tools Switch Sides
hook: Doctrines aren't ideologies. Watch one Supreme Court term closely and you can see arguments long branded conservative being made by liberals, and vice versa.
key_points: SCOTUSblog's Richard Re describes an October Term 2025 'realignment': positions once associated with the right now argued by the left, and the reverse.
Originalism is the clearest case — scholar Larry Solum counted only Justice Thomas using a primarily originalist method in two major separation-of-powers cases.
Re calls novel substantive due process rights enforced by the conservative majority the biggest single realignment of the year.
Justice Sotomayor now defends stare decisis in dissent, quoting her own 2021 dissent on how far respect for precedent has fallen.
In a tariffs case the liberal justices argued from the plain statutory text while conservatives built atextual doctrine around it.
Even justiciability moved: a 6-3 mootness split had all conservatives on one side and all liberals on the other, reversing the historical pattern.
content_html: It is tempting to file legal doctrines under political labels: originalism on the right, living-constitutionalism on the left, stare decisis somewhere in between. Reviewing October Term 2025 for SCOTUSblog, Richard Re argues the labels have come loose. His term-in-review describes a "realignment" in which, as he puts it, legal views once associated with the right are now espoused by the left, and vice versa.
extra_html:
The examples span six areas. In two major separation-of-powers cases, the majority opinion read as pragmatic rather than originalist — originalism scholar Larry Solum counted only Justice Thomas employing a primarily originalist method. The conservative majority enforced a novel substantive due process right, a doctrine Justice Scalia spent a career attacking, which Re calls the year's biggest single realignment. Justice Alito's dissent in a citizenship case invoked British, Mexican, Guatemalan and Chinese law — the sort of comparative argument conservatives long condemned. Justice Sotomayor, dissenting, lamented "how low this Court's respect for stare decisis has sunk," quoting herself from 2021. In the tariffs case the liberal justices held to the statute's text while the majority built doctrine above it. And on justiciability, a 6-3 mootness split put all conservatives on one side and all liberals on the other, inverting the traditional alignment.

The transferable lesson is that interpretive methods are tools, and tools get picked up by whoever needs them. A doctrine that constrains the government is attractive to whichever side is out of power; a doctrine that unsettles precedent is attractive to whichever side wants change. Re's summary of the drift: "Once again, Breyer's legacy improbably gains ground over Scalia's."

related.title: Beyond the Swing Justice
related.hook: The 'swing vote' is a lazy model of a nine-member court. Sort four terms of close cases and you get two distinct jobs: building narrow majorities, and bridging the dissents nobody won.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: The Power of a Dissent
related.hook: A dissenting judge loses the case — but a sharp dissent can outlive the majority, persuading future courts or pushing lawmakers to rewrite the rule.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

related.title: Nine Justices, Nine Styles
related.hook: One scholar coded 5,095 questions from a full Supreme Court term and found each justice interrogates lawyers in a signature way — a fingerprint of how they think about the law.

flashcards.prompt: What does Re mean by 'realignment' on the Supreme Court?
flashcards.back_html: Not a change in who wins, but in which side uses which legal tool — methods like originalism, textualism and stare decisis migrating from the justices who championed them to those who once resisted them.

flashcards.prompt: Which pattern would count as evidence of realignment in this sense?

choices.text: Liberal justices insisting on a plain reading of the statute while conservatives build doctrine around it
A 6-3 ruling splitting exactly along ideological lines
The Court agreeing unanimously in a low-profile case

flashcards.explanation_html: Realignment is about method, not outcome. Textualism argued by the liberal wing against an atextual conservative doctrine is precisely the swap Re tracks.

flashcards.prompt: Why is it a mistake to treat a doctrine like stare decisis as inherently conservative or liberal?
flashcards.back_html: Procedural and interpretive tools favor whoever benefits from the status quo at the time. As majorities change, so does which side finds each tool useful.
